speakers: Andrew Beer (co-founder DBi, managed-futures replication ETF DBMF)
summary:
Systematic Investor weekly with Beer and Kaastrup-Larsen (Sept 2025). Topics: inelastic market hypothesis and breaking 60/40 paradigm, Sept 2025 CTA performance and the 'let it run hot' trade, why replication outperformed large single-manager CTAs in 2024-25 (implementability, liquidity, whipsaw), and why multistrategy pod hedge funds deliver consistent returns.
Main conclusions: flows and paradigm shifts matter, cost/liquidity limit broad universes, multistrats work via talent plus structure but face capacity risk.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the um equities are up 55% over that period of time and uh and and and nothing's broken
claims.claim: Despite a long list of political, war and tariff shocks over ~2 years, equities rallied about 55%, showing the system's resilience, though Beer thinks repeated shocks cannot be ignored forever.
claims.conditions: after repeated shocks without a market break; Beer expects fragility eventually

claims.speaker: Neils Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: inelastic market hypothesis um where essentially it's a theory that um contemplates that $1 into equities just it doesn't just notch the price higher
claims.claim: Under the inelastic market hypothesis (Bouchaud/CFM), each dollar flowing into equities moves price by a multiple of that dollar because few participants absorb flow, so flows rather than fundamentals can dominate returns.
claims.indicator: net equity fund flows / price impact multiplier
claims.direction: equity prices rise with inflows, fall with outflows
claims.testable: yes - price impact of flows can be estimated

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: if you are the very best executive in America running a steel company going through a 30-year structural decline, you're going to have a really hard time
claims.claim: Skill is only monetised where the opportunity set is favourable; talent cannot overcome a structurally declining or efficient area, so market efficiency varies by segment.
claims.conditions: depends on the market segment's opportunity

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: when you have an existing paradigm, it it's very sticky because you have tons and tons of people who are trained in that paradigm
claims.claim: Investment paradigms (e.g. efficient markets, Black-Litterman allocation) persist until contradicting evidence reaches critical mass, because practitioners' identity is tied to them, so paradigm change is slow then abrupt.

claims.speaker: Neils Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: what determines more uh what goes on in markets are the flows, right?
claims.claim: If market outcomes are driven mainly by flows, a reversal of passive inflows could produce a very different market regime from the post-GFC rally.
claims.testable: partly - flow data exist but regime shift is a prediction

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: if you'd done it in 1990, um then you wouldn't have seen the same negative correlation or zero correlation of stocks and bonds
claims.claim: 60/40 worked because of the stock-bond correlation regime of the long bond bull market (zero/negative correlation); it reinforced itself as a paradigm and would not have looked the same starting in 1990.
claims.testable: yes - rolling correlation and 60/40 results by start date

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: bonds have 80 80% correlation to equities and they went down in 2020 when they were supposed to protect
claims.claim: This decade bonds became highly correlated with equities (around 0.8 in his words, vol doubled or tripled) and fell with stocks in the inflation shock, breaking the diversification premise of 60/40.
claims.direction: bonds fail to hedge equities in an inflation regime

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: equity long short was everyone's favorite hedge fund strategy in the 2000s. by the end of the 2010s it had faced years and years and years of underperformance
claims.claim: Passive investing may have impaired some active strategies such as equity long/short, while others such as managed futures are affected differently, so the impact is uneven.
claims.testable: partly - attribution to passive is hard

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: it presented an opportunity for CTAs to make a decade of alpha in one year
claims.claim: Allocators who deliberately do not change their minds quickly were slow to react when inflation returned, so fast trend followers made about a decade of alpha in 2022.
claims.direction: long managed futures/trend when inflation regime shifts
claims.conditions: when allocators and portfolios are slow to adapt to a regime change

claims.speaker: Neils Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: If if money starts to flow out of passive funds and we get a 10-year bare market, everyone's gonna love short sellers again.
claims.claim: If passive funds see outflows and a long bear market arrives, allocator demand for dedicated short sellers would reverse from nil to high.
claims.conditions: in a prolonged bear market with passive outflows

claims.speaker: Neils Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: every investment is judged by its contribution ution to the entire portfolio goals, not just its own asset class
claims.claim: Under CalPERS' total portfolio approach, assets are judged by contribution to total portfolio goals, which would favour diversifiers such as trend following that look unappealing on a standalone basis.
claims.direction: more allocation to diversifying strategies like managed futures
claims.conditions: if institutions follow through; may take years to trickle down
claims.testable: partly - portfolio contribution can be tested

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they torture the data until they get the the answer that they want
claims.claim: Capital market assumption and asset allocation models fit historical premia (e.g. size factor with data issues in 2000) and extrapolate them, so results are overfit and judgement is layered on top.
claims.testable: yes - out-of-sample test of extrapolated assumptions

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: they kind of haircut assumptions for things that look too good recently and they and they kind of assume mean reversion on other assets
claims.claim: Institutional allocators haircut recent winners (e.g. Nasdaq) and assume mean reversion for others, so they are structurally unlikely to give large allocations to whatever has recently worked.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we basically decided in the beginning of 2021 that a very meaningful portion of your portfolio would be in something that mathematically was going to diff have difficulty earning a return over time
claims.claim: Holding a large bond allocation at the peak of the bond bubble (2021 yields) mathematically limited future returns, a mistake of the 60/40 paradigm.
claims.direction: bonds' expected return low when yields are low
claims.testable: yes - starting yield predicts bond returns

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: a lot of people who um who who sold or built their business on 60/40 have now introduced a 20% % diversifying bucket
claims.claim: US wealth managers moved from 60/40 to 60/20/20 with a 20% diversifying bucket because bonds had correlation to equities of about 0.8, vol up 2-3x and returned less than cash.

claims.speaker: Neils Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: It's the equities and it's the precious metals in particular uh that are helping with a few supporting acts from the commodity side
claims.claim: In September 2025 trend following profits came from equities and precious metals, while fixed income was quiet despite the Fed pivot.

claims.speaker: Neils Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: The trend index is up almost 5% for the month um as of Tuesday, I should say. Um down 3% for the year.
claims.claim: As of late September 2025 the trend index was up almost 5% for the month but down 3% YTD, while MSCI World was up about 17% and S&P 500 about 14%.
claims.indicator: SG Trend Index; SG CTA Index; BUP 50; short-term traders index

claims.speaker: Neils Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my own trend barometer finished at 36 yesterday
claims.claim: Kaastrup-Larsen's trend barometer read 36 (weak) despite good performance data; a fourth positive month for SG Trend would be the first since Jan-Apr 2024.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: BTFD
claims.claim: Beer advised a client near the lows to buy the dip because trend following has a known pattern of being rattled and then turning around and pivoting.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: what I think it detected early was the let it run hot trade
claims.claim: After the April 2025 Liberation Day whipsaw, trend models detected the let-it-run-hot trade early (long equities/gold/crypto) even when it felt reckless in June.
claims.direction: long equities, gold, crypto; short USD

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: Fed is Trump is going to jawbone the Fed or they're going to then keep rates lower than they should that's going to you drive up equity valuations.
claims.claim: Let-it-run-hot view: political pressure keeps rates lower than warranted, lifting equity valuations and gold/crypto, with a bond tantrum later rather than sooner; the president is also structurally short the dollar.
claims.direction: long equities, gold, crypto; bond tantrum later
claims.conditions: while Fed is pressured to stay easy

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we have about a 300 basis point efficiency advantage
claims.claim: Pair trading replication against single managers is costly because replication has historically had about a 300 bps annual cost advantage over hedge fund CTAs, so the short side bleeds, and timing relative outperformance is unpredictable.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you could buy five well-known mutual funds in the US and short DBMF against it and you'd lose 300 basis points on average
claims.claim: Hedging or pairing against replication loses at least 300 bps per year on average; for investable mutual fund or UCITS managed futures the gap is greater than 300 bps.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we didn't have the Mexican peso, we didn't have the front end of the Canadian interest rate curve, we didn't have the Nikkay, we didn't have softs
claims.claim: Replication underperforms when many idiosyncratic non-core trades (Mexican peso, Canada front end, Nikkei, softs in early 2023) work at the same time, which is hard to forecast.
claims.conditions: when a broad set of niche markets trend together
claims.testable: yes - attribute replication tracking error to markets absent

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: when it keeps going we will be de-risking that position faster than actual funds
claims.claim: At sharp inflection points like SVB (March 2023), replication loses a few hundred bps at most when a sharp reversal persists and gets de-risked faster than actual funds, but recovers if it was a head fake.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the periods when we tend to outperform are periods when those non-core trades backfire or risk management backfire
claims.claim: Replication outperforms when the extra non-core trades or the risk management overlays of single-manager CTAs backfire.

claims.speaker: Neils Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: I would argue that there have been you know two three big reversals in all of those sectors within the last 14 months
claims.claim: Large CTAs tilted to financials suffered because equities, fixed income and currencies each had 2-3 large reversals within about 14 months, forcing long/short flips (whipsaw).
claims.conditions: when all financial sectors reverse together
claims.testable: yes - trend returns vs reversal frequency

claims.speaker: Neils Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: those that are more diversified where smaller market contributions or where smaller markets like you know the commodities have been able to mitigate um some of those losses
claims.claim: Managers with broader diversification including commodities mitigated losses from financial sector reversals.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: 80 to 90% of ETFs are outperforming um the average mutual fund hedge fund in 2024 and 2025 by a lot
claims.claim: In 2024-2025 the large majority of simple ETF replication products beat the average mutual fund/hedge fund managed futures peer, which should not happen and suggests a structural reason.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: in a four or five day period of time, you may be selling a hundred different positions or buying back a 100 different positions in markets where there's thin liquidity
claims.claim: Large multi-hundred-instrument CTAs with vol controls and short-term models must trade many positions in thin markets after shocks, incurring large impact costs and whipsaw.
claims.conditions: after shocks when liquidity vanishes in large footprint

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: you're also trading with prop desks, right? Who can who can smell blood in the water.
claims.claim: CTAs exiting positions in stressed illiquid markets trade against prop desks that anticipate forced flows, adding to cost.
claims.conditions: during forced selling in thin markets

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: would you five years ago when you thought about in including position number 298 would you have included in your portfolio knowing there could be a day where you lost 200 basis points just trading it
claims.claim: Before adding a marginal market to a CTA portfolio, test whether a stress-day execution loss (e.g. 200 bps) would have justified inclusion; liquidity under stress should be a market-selection criterion.

claims.speaker: Neils Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: all markets has the ability to trend. They obviously don't trend at the same time
claims.claim: Every market can trend but not simultaneously, so broad diversification will sometimes lag a narrower longer-timeframe replication, yet the 2024-25 snapshot is not conclusive evidence of a permanent change.
claims.conditions: periods where niche markets do not trend

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: If getting in and out costs you 10 to 15%. brokerage commissions and everything else, there may be a trend, you still don't want to try to do it from an investment perspective.
claims.claim: A trend only has value if transaction costs allow capture (Copenhagen housing example): trendfollowing needs low costs.
claims.testable: yes - net of cost trend returns

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the returns disappeared at 30 or 50 million
claims.claim: Strategies like high-frequency trading earned huge returns on a few million dollars but alpha disappeared at 30-50 million, so capacity and implementation limit what backtests suggest.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: what do you think about trading 300 instruments, not 70?
claims.claim: Slippage measured on simple 70-market liquid portfolios may not hold when trading 300 instruments; quants once boasted of cutting slippage from 400 to 200 bps.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: everybody evaluates these things on the very worst day that it can happen.
claims.claim: Allocators judge strategies by worst-day outcomes, e.g. private credit risk lies in defaults and markdowns, so execution and liquidity must be evaluated for stress scenarios.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: that recovery is not necessarily a sign of long-term high expected returns
claims.claim: The rebound in managers after April 2025 may reflect a liquidity influx (YOLO, FOMO, let it run hot) rather than durable expected returns.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: the worst month I've been able to find was down 6% in March
claims.claim: Multistrategy hedge funds had a worst month of -6% in March 2020 (about -1% at 5x unleveraged equivalent) while delivering consistent returns.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: 2% in 2022 up 6% in 23 up 11% 24 and up 8% year-to- date.
claims.claim: Pivotal Path Multistrategy index returns: 2020 13%, 2021 9%, 2022 2%, 2023 6%, 2024 11%, 2025 YTD 8%, very steady, with total fees possibly 1000 bps before clients are paid.
claims.indicator: Pivotal Path Multistrategy Hedge Fund Index
claims.testable: yes - index data from CalPERS-type institutions

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: He's going to do 30 a year for his first three years.
claims.claim: Giving an exceptional specialist manager seed capital with capacity caps and full fees yields about 30% a year for the first three years, because new talented managers outperform before size grows.
claims.conditions: provided AUM growth is capped and managed accounts give transparency

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: Banks used to pay 55% of revenue
claims.claim: Multistrat funds act like bank proprietary desks with better information, financing and pay-out around 55% of revenue as compensation.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: picking uh large cap stocks in the US and getting paid 100 basis points for it, your clients are probably not you're probably not going to do better than 100 basis points over time statistically
claims.claim: Markets are efficient in segments like US large cap stocks, so fees of 100 bps are not recouped, but esoteric segments remain inefficient where talent can earn alpha.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: we can take that guy and give him an incentive structure where he is not sleeping for the next five years
claims.claim: Multistrats bet that putting top PMs in a structure removing distractions with high payouts (e.g. $200m of $500m profit) leaves clients, firm and PM better off.

claims.speaker: Neils Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the risk management teams that are allocating the money to these uh sub uh parts to a large extent they're buying P&L curves
claims.claim: Multistrats allocate capital to pods mainly by past P&L, which risks capacity dilution and hidden leverage as inflows grow, as in private equity.
claims.conditions: as assets grow and leverage increases

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: is is pod number 300 right by definition less attractive than pod number 20
claims.claim: Marginal pods are logically less attractive than earlier ones, so capacity dilution is a risk for multistrats, although leaders like Citadel have so far disproved it.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: not a single one of these funds had not only not blown up, but not had a anything approaching what would be deemed to be a catastrophic draw down
claims.claim: Despite 5x leverage on $50bn and major regime shifts since 2020, no multistrat blew up or had a catastrophic drawdown, which suggests the pod structure with hedge fund format works.
claims.conditions: needs hedge fund structure with lockups

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: has been an embarrassing failure. the the entire space has done less than 3% peranom after about a 200 basis points in in in expenses over the past 10 years
claims.claim: Liquid-alt multi-strategy mutual funds, the plug-and-play versions, returned under 3% a year over 10 years after about 200 bps of fees, and cannot replicate hedge fund multistrats with quarterly liquidity.
claims.conditions: needs hedge fund structure with limited withdrawals

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: being down 3% one year and, you know, he goes back to his office and the fact his, you know, he's he's all his stuff is sitting in boxes
claims.claim: Pod managers face harsh drawdown limits, a down 3% year can mean dismissal, which drives risk discipline and hunger.

claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
claims.quote: generate a four sharp ratio, take two of the sharp ratio to pay everybody
claims.claim: Paying 1000 bps in fees is acceptable if the pod structure generates a Sharpe near 4 and half is paid out, but 200 bps for a 3% multi-strategy mutual fund return is excessive.
